## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Duddubhajātaka* (Ja 322; alternatively spelled *Daddabhajātaka*) is a story belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [Anandajoti 2010]. According to its opening nidāna, the framing story was related by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana concerning a group of heretics.

The narrative relates the well-known fable of a hare who hears the sound of a falling fruit—commented upon as a ripe bael fruit (*beluvapakka*) falling with a thud (*duddubha* / *dabhakka*)—and panics under the delusion that the world is ending [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The hare's flight triggers widespread panic among a vast multitude of animals (*migavāhinī*), until the Bodhisatta investigates the source of the commotion and calms the beasts [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The concluding verses (*abhisambuddhagāthā*) observe that fools who heed rumors without discerning the truth succumb to negligence and hearsay (*paraghosānusārino*), whereas virtuous and wise practitioners who find peace through discernment remain unaffected by external panic [Fausböll 1883].
